items.title: Assurance and the three lines
items.source: HM Treasury, The Orange Book: Management of Risk; Government Internal Audit Standards
items.body: Assurance is independent confidence that work is on track and controls are working. A common model describes three lines. In the first line, managers run the service and operate the controls. In the second line, specialist functions such as risk, finance and compliance set the rules and monitor how they are applied. In the third line, internal audit gives an independent view to the board and audit committee on whether risk management and controls are effective. Internal audit must be independent of the work it examines and reports to the audit committee, so it can speak plainly. It advises and reports, but managers stay responsible for fixing the issues.

options.text: Independent confidence that work is on track and controls are working

questions.prompt: Which line of defence is internal audit?
Why must internal audit be independent of the work it examines?

options.text: So it can approve its own recommendations
So it has no access to records
So it can give an objective view and report plainly to the audit committee
So it can run the project instead

questions.prompt: A delivery manager asks internal audit to design and approve the controls for their new process before the audit begins. What is the issue and what should happen?
questions.answer: Internal audit cannot design and then independently audit the same controls; that would compromise independence. The manager, with the risk or finance function, should design the controls. Internal audit can give advice in general terms and later audit them objectively.
questions.rubric: Should say independence is compromised if audit designs/approves controls it later audits; managers own control design with second line support; audit reviews afterwards.

items.title: Gateway reviews and delivery assurance
items.source: Infrastructure and Projects Authority / Cabinet Office, Gateway review guidance
items.body: Gateway reviews are short independent reviews of major projects and programmes at key points. Gateway 0 assesses the strategic case, Gateway 1 the business justification, Gateway 2 the delivery strategy, Gateway 3 the investment decision, Gateway 4 readiness for service and Gateway 5 operations and benefits. Reviewers give a delivery confidence assessment using five ratings from green to red, where red means successful delivery appears unachievable and major issues need action. The review is confidential and helps the senior responsible owner. The right response to an unwelcome rating is an action plan with owners and dates, not an argument about the colour.

options.text: A meeting to launch a project
A short independent review of a major project at a key point

questions.prompt: Which Gateway review looks at the investment decision?
What does a Red delivery confidence assessment indicate?

options.text: Successful delivery appears unachievable and major issues need action
The review has not been completed

questions.prompt: A review rates your programme Amber/Red. The sponsor wants to argue the rating is unfair. What do you advise?
questions.answer: Treat the findings seriously: correct any factual errors with the reviewers, but focus on the recommendations. Agree an action plan with owners and dates, report progress to the board and ask for a follow-up review. Arguing about the rating wastes the time needed to fix the problems.
questions.rubric: Should advise accepting findings, correcting facts only, building a dated action plan with owners, escalating and reporting progress, follow-up review.

items.title: Scrutiny, committees and external audit
items.source: National Audit Office; Public Accounts Committee; Local Government Act 2000
items.body: In central government, the National Audit Office (NAO), led by the Comptroller and Auditor General, audits departments' accounts and examines value for money, reporting to Parliament. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) uses NAO reports to question senior officials about how money was used. In English local government, overview and scrutiny committees hold the executive to account, can review policy and can use call-in, which asks the decision makers to reconsider a decision before it is carried out. Appearing before a committee calls for accurate evidence, clear ownership of decisions, honesty about what went wrong and a follow-up on what has been done.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the Public Accounts Committee?

options.text: To examine the value for money of government spending, using NAO reports

questions.prompt: Who leads the National Audit Office?

options.text: The Permanent Secretary of the Treasury

questions.prompt: What does call-in allow a scrutiny committee to do?

options.text: Ask the executive to reconsider a decision before it is implemented
Cancel a decision on its own authority

questions.prompt: You are asked to prepare an accounting officer for a committee hearing on a large overspend. How would you help them prepare?
questions.answer: Gather the facts and timeline, confirm who made each decision, be candid about what went wrong and what has been done to fix it, prepare short clear answers and supporting evidence, anticipate difficult questions and agree follow-up actions and a timetable for any written evidence.
questions.rubric: Should include facts and timeline, accountability for decisions, candour, concise answers with evidence, anticipating questions, and follow-up actions.

items.title: Benefits and closure assurance
items.source: HM Treasury, Green Book; Cabinet Office, project delivery guidance
items.body: Benefits assurance checks that the benefits promised in the business case are being delivered, who owns them, how they are measured and whether the measures still make sense. A post-implementation review, normally done some months after launch, compares what happened with the case. Closure assurance is a last independent check that the work has closed properly: contracts ended, assets and data dealt with, staff supported, risks closed or handed on, and lessons recorded. Lessons are only useful if they are shared, someone is responsible for acting on them, and they are checked at the start of the next project.

options.text: That the project is on budget only
That promised benefits are being delivered and are measured
That the project should start again
That the work has closed properly, with contracts, data, assets and risks dealt with
They are written but not read
They are kept by the project manager only
They are shared, owned and checked at the start of future projects

questions.prompt: A post-implementation review 18 months after launch finds that only 40% of the promised benefits have been delivered. What do you recommend?
questions.answer: Understand which benefits are missing and why: unrealistic targets, no owner, or delivery failure. Agree actions with owners for those that can still be achieved, update the benefits plan and business case, report honestly to the board, and record lessons for future cases.
questions.rubric: Should investigate causes, assign owners and actions, update the plan/case, report honestly, and capture lessons.
